q: A student wants to know how far a vineyard sits from the equator, and finds two sets of lines printed across the globe. Which set answers the question?
opts: The tropics and the polar circles
The lines marking the time zones
exp: Parallels run east to west and are numbered from zero at the equator to ninety at each pole, so a vineyard's latitude is its distance from the equator stated in degrees. Meridians run the other way and measure how far east or west a place lies, which settles its clock and tells you nothing about its climate.

q: Most of Germany's vineyard sits between roughly forty-seven and fifty-two degrees north, among the coolest latitudes carrying classic wine regions. What does that position do to the sunlight?
opts: It removes the risk of spring frost
It lifts the sun overhead at midday, so level ground gathers the most energy
It lengthens the ripening season by roughly two months in an average year
It keeps the sun low, so ground tilted toward it gathers more energy
exp: At a low sun angle the same beam of light is smeared across a wide patch of flat ground. Tilting the ground toward the sun concentrates it again, which is why Germany's best sites are also its steepest.

q: Growers on the Rhine and the Mosel plant as close to the water as the slope allows, and abandon the ground once it climbs away from the bank. What are the rivers giving them?
opts: Humidity high enough to prevent fungal disease
Cool air that holds budbreak back until the frost risk has passed
Irrigation water permitted under German wine law
Reflected light, stored warmth that blunts frost, and a longer autumn
exp: A large body of water warms and cools slowly, so the river carries heat into the autumn and takes the edge off the coldest nights. Its surface also throws light back up onto the slope above it.

q: Dark Devonian rock along the Mosel absorbs heat through the day and gives it back after sunset. What is it?
exp: Slate is dark enough to warm quickly and splits into plates that drain hard and hold no water. On a cold October night the stone is still radiating the afternoon back at the fruit.

q: The Mosel doubles back on itself again and again on its way to the Rhine. Why does that serpentine course matter so much to a grower?
opts: Each bend forms a separate appellation under German law
Every bend gives a different aspect, and only some ripen Riesling
The bends slow the current and raise humidity enough to guarantee noble rot
The loops shorten the distance the fruit must travel to the cellar
exp: A single meander presents every point of the compass within a couple of kilometres. The famous sites are the ones caught on the steep southern flank of a bend, and the ground facing them is often left unplanted.

q: Vines on the steepest Mosel ground are each trained up a single tall stake rather than along a wire trellis. What forces that?
opts: Stakes shelter the vine from wind coming off the river
German law requires stake training for Pradikatswein
The slope is too steep to work along a contour
A stake carries more fruit per vine than a wire
exp: Einzelpfahl training lets a worker move vertically, which is the only practical direction on ground of forty or fifty degrees. Every operation is done by hand, and that cost is built into the price of the bottle.

q: Nothing on the steepest slate slopes can be worked by tractor or machine harvester. What follows from that for the wine?
opts: The wine must legally be sold as Landwein or Tafelwein
Labour costs many times more, setting a price floor
Fermentation has to be carried out in the vineyard itself
Yields run far higher than on flat land
exp: Hand pruning, hand picking and carrying eroded soil back up the hill in baskets all have to be paid for, which sets a floor under what the wine must sell for. Where the market will not carry that cost the vineyards are simply abandoned, and many fine sites have been.

q: A German quality wine must name on its label whichever of the thirteen official growing regions it came from. What are those regions called?
exp: The Anbaugebiet is the top administrative unit; a Bereich is a district inside one, and a Grosslage a collective site inside that. Qualitatswein and Pradikatswein must both carry the Anbaugebiet name.

q: Which German region is unusual in planting more red than white, with Trollinger and Lemberger at the centre of it?
exp: Wurttemberg drinks most of what it makes, and Trollinger, the grape the Alto Adige calls Schiava, is its everyday red. Lemberger, which Austria knows as Blaufrankisch, is the serious one.

q: One German region lies far to the south, facing Alsace across the Rhine, and is the warmest of the thirteen. Which?
exp: Baden is long and narrow, running from the Bodensee up to Heidelberg. Its warmth is why the Pinot family rather than Riesling dominates there, in the shape of Spatburgunder, Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder.

q: A tiny northerly region on a left-bank tributary of the Rhine gives itself over almost entirely to red wine, which is remarkable that far north. Which one?
exp: The Ahr valley is narrow, steep and floored with slate, and it traps enough heat to ripen Spatburgunder at fifty degrees north. Fruhburgunder, an early-ripening mutation of the same grape, is its other speciality.

q: Two German regions sit far to the east on the Saale and the Elbe, and spent forty years cut off from the western wine trade. Which pair?
exp: Both are among the smallest and most northerly of the thirteen, and both lay inside East Germany until 1990. They work steep terraces and bottle almost everything dry.

q: Riesling from Mosel slate often reaches the table at seven or eight percent alcohol. What keeps a wine that light from tasting thin?
opts: A long spell in oak before bottling
exp: The cool site leaves the acidity intact and the fermentation is stopped with sugar still in the wine. Sweetness and acid balance one another, so the wine reads as delicate rather than watery.

q: Two tributaries joining the Mosel near Trier were once named alongside it in the region's full title. Which?
exp: The Saar is cooler and steelier than the main valley and the Ruwer smaller and lighter still. The whole region was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer before the name was shortened to Mosel.

q: The Mosel's best-known individual site clings to the slate directly above one town and carries a physician's name from a legend about a cured archbishop. Which vineyard?
exp: The story has an Archbishop of Trier recovering from a fever after drinking it, and the site is a narrow strip of steep slate right behind the town. It is a byword for expensive vineyard land in Germany.

q: Slate is not all one colour along the Mosel. Which village is known for weathered red slate and volcanic sandstone giving unusually spicy, exotic Riesling?
exp: The Wurzgarten, the spice garden, sits on red rock rather than the blue-grey slate of Wehlen and Graach upstream. Its wines are broader and more perfumed, and they smell of the name.
